lead: The engine is a control loop of its own. The thrust lever states a demand; the engine control system sets fuel flow and engine geometry to meet it while keeping spool speeds, exhaust gas temperature and surge margin inside limits. Older engines use hydro-mechanical fuel control units; modern ones use a Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC). The same loop accepts thrust demand from the auto-throttle and returns engine data to the cockpit. Some syllabi teach it with flight controls, because it is a clear example of a fast inner loop nested under the auto-throttle.
prereq: You need: the chapter on autopilots for auto-throttle, and the closed-loop idea from the chapter on powered flight controls and the chapter on digital fly-by-wire.

blocks.text: An engine control loop has one thrust-setting variable and several limits. On most turbofans the thrust parameter is N1, the low-pressure or fan spool speed as a percentage of a reference. Some engines use N2, the high-pressure spool speed, or the engine pressure ratio (EPR) as the thrust-setting parameter; the rest of the loop is the same. EGT is the exhaust gas temperature; TGT (turbine gas temperature) is the same kind of measurement taken closer to the turbine, so its limiting value differs from the EGT limit. P1 and T1 are inlet pressure and temperature, because air density changes how much fuel a lever setting should receive. Fuel flow is in kg/s, and oil pressure is a health input.

An engine control acts on three things: fuel flow (the fuel metering valve), air flow (variable stator vanes and compressor bleed valves, which keep the compressor away from surge) and, on some engines, the exhaust (nozzle area on afterburning military engines, and the thrust reverser). A hydro-mechanical fuel control unit (FCU) does the fuel part with cams, bellows, levers and a flyweight speed governor: the lever sets the governed speed, and the governor meters fuel to hold it. During a rapid lever movement an acceleration schedule caps the fuel flow, because too much fuel at once would push the compressor into surge or over-heat the turbine; a deceleration schedule keeps a minimum flow so the flame does not go out. Limiters cut fuel before EGT or spool speed passes its limit. The FCU is reliable but hard to retune, and it has no software and no built-in test. Ignition and the thrust reverser are separate systems on such an engine.

A FADEC (Full Authority Digital Engine Control) is an electronic engine control with two channels, one active and one standby. It has its own power supply, built-in test, and no full-authority mechanical backup. It reads throttle lever angle, N1, N2, EGT, fuel flow, P1, T1 and oil pressure, then drives the fuel metering valve, stator vanes, bleed valves and ignition. It also runs auto-start and sends engine data to the cockpit and the auto-throttle.

The lever asks for a rating, not a fuel flow. Typical ratings are take-off, maximum continuous, climb and cruise. For each rating the FADEC computes a target N1 from the inlet conditions P1 and T1 and holds it by trimming fuel. The target is set as a corrected speed, because the fan and compressor behave the same at the same N1 ÷ √θ.

blocks.where: N1<sub>c</sub> is the corrected fan speed in % (what the rating fixes); N1 is the physical fan speed in %; θ is the inlet temperature ratio; T1 is the inlet total temperature in kelvin; 288.15 K is the sea-level standard temperature.

blocks.text: On a hot day the same corrected speed needs a higher physical N1 and runs a higher EGT. When a physical limit is reached, FADEC holds the limit and the thrust falls, so the same lever position gives different thrust on a hot afternoon and a cold morning. In automatic flight the flight control system sends thrust demand to the auto-throttle, which moves the lever; FADEC still decides the fuel.

figure.caption: The FADEC loop, and the worked example’s take-off rating held as corrected fan speed 97.0 %. The physical N1 needed is 92.7 % at −10 °C and 97.0 % at 15 °C; at 40 °C the schedule asks for 101.1 %, so the FADEC holds the 100.0 % limit and thrust falls.

Bottom: bar chart of physical N1 for three inlet temperatures: 92.7 percent at minus 10 degrees, 97.0 at 15, and 100.0 at 40, where 101.1 was asked, under a dashed 100 percent limit line.

examples.question: A FADEC sets the take-off rating as a corrected fan speed N1<sub>c</sub> = 97.0 %. The physical N1 limit is 100.0 %. Find the physical N1 the FADEC commands at an inlet temperature of (a) 15 °C, (b) −10 °C and (c) 40 °C. (d) At 40 °C, what corrected speed can the engine actually reach?
steps: Use N1 = N1<sub>c</sub> × √θ with θ = T1 ÷ 288.15 K, temperatures in kelvin.
(c) 40 °C = 313.15 K: θ = 313.15 ÷ 288.15 = 1.0868, √θ = 1.0425, so the schedule asks for 97.0 × 1.0425 = 101.1 %. That is above the 100.0 % limit, so the FADEC holds N1 at 100.0 %.
(d) At the limit, N1<sub>c</sub> = 100.0 ÷ 1.0425 = 95.9 %, below the 97.0 % rating, so take-off thrust is lower on the hot day.
examples.answer: N1 is 97.0 % at 15 °C and 92.7 % at −10 °C; at 40 °C the schedule asks for 101.1 %, the FADEC holds the 100.0 % limit, and the corrected speed reached is only 95.9 %, so take-off thrust falls.

traps: FADEC does not move the thrust lever; the lever is the pilot's or auto-throttle's demand.
N1 is the fan or low-pressure spool and normally sets thrust; N2 is the high-pressure spool.
EGT is a limit, not the thrust-setting parameter: on a hot day the engine reaches its EGT or N1 limit at a lower thrust.
Using °C in θ = T1 ÷ 288.15. Use kelvin: 40 °C is 313.15 K, so θ = 1.0868.
A rating is a thrust schedule, not a fixed fuel flow.

quiz.a: The low-pressure or fan spool speed, shown as a percentage of a reference.

quiz.q: Why does FADEC need P1 and T1?
quiz.a: Inlet pressure and temperature set air density; the N1 schedule and fuel need change with them.

quiz.q: What does 'full authority' mean in FADEC?
quiz.a: It controls fuel and engine geometry over the whole operating range, with no separate hydromechanical fuel control in normal operation.

quiz.q: Fuel flow is 0.15 kg/s for 30 minutes. Find the mass.
The lever is unchanged but thrust falls on a hot day. Explain.
quiz.a: FADEC schedules N1 for inlet temperature and trims fuel at the EGT limit, so the same lever gives less thrust.
One active, one standby, so a single electronic failure does not lose engine control.

quiz.q: How does the automatic flight control system use FADEC?
quiz.a: It sends thrust demand to the auto-throttle, which moves the lever; FADEC turns lever position into fuel and limits.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern engines add model-based control and engine health monitoring: FADEC data trends fan speed, EGT and fuel flow to predict maintenance before a fault. The same data feeds the cockpit and the airline's ground system. Newer work links the engine and flight control loops more tightly for drag reduction and quieter climbs. Search next for FADEC, N1 schedule, engine health monitoring and auto-throttle integration.
